title: Surface Area of Prisms and Cylinders

findings.finding: Generalise the number of faces of a right prism from its end polygon.
findings.breakdown: The task asks students to explain the structure already visible in the polygonal prism nets, including concave ends.
findings.checked: p3-identify-b, p3-identify-c, p3-identify-g and p3-identify-h show one lateral rectangle per polygon side and two matching ends. The proposed counts are correct.
findings.assumptions: The end polygon is simple and non-degenerate, with n sides.

repair.proposal: After p4-q4, optionally ask: 'A right prism has an end polygon with n sides. How many rectangular lateral faces and how many faces altogether does it have? Explain why. Does your rule still work if the polygon has an inward notch?' Expected answer: n lateral rectangles and n + 2 faces altogether; each polygon side produces one rectangle, and there are two matching ends. A concave end does not change this count.

findings.doneWhen: Students explain the face count using the correspondence between polygon sides and lateral rectangles.

findings.finding: The opening teaching uses rectangular area without a review rehearsing it.
findings.breakdown: Each face-pair calculation requires selecting two rectangular dimensions and multiplying them. Weak recall can prevent students from understanding the products as face areas.
findings.checked: p5-example-solid-column directly uses rectangular area three times. The preceding nets teaching and p4-q4 identify solids and faces without calculating areas. No opening review supplies this prerequisite.
findings.assumptions: Rectangle area is prior knowledge. Teacher-led checking can identify and address recall gaps. Calculator availability does not affect this finding.

repair.proposal: Before p5-definition-block, add: 'Find each rectangle's area. Write the calculation and include units. a Length 7 cm, width 4 cm. b Length 9 mm, width 3 mm. c Length 5 m, width 8 m.' Expected answers: 28 cm², 27 mm² and 40 m².

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse rectangular area before following the face-area products.

findings.finding: The triangular-prism topic uses triangle area without reviewing its formula and perpendicular height.
findings.breakdown: Students must halve the base–height product and select the perpendicular height rather than a sloping side. Failure at either step changes both triangular end areas.
findings.checked: p14-example-triangles uses base 6 cm and perpendicular height 4 cm while the diagram also supplies sloping sides of 5 cm. Earlier triangular-area practice occurs in the surface-area-nets topic, but the immediately preceding rectangular-prism topic does not rehearse it.
findings.assumptions: Triangle area is prior knowledge, supported by the separate Area of Parallelograms and Triangles booklet. This finding does not depend on calculator use.

repair.proposal: Before p14-example-block, add: '1 Complete: Area of a triangle = __ × base × perpendicular height. 2 An isosceles triangle has base 8 cm, perpendicular height 3 cm and equal sloping sides 5 cm. Which lengths belong in the area formula? Find its area. 3 A right triangle has perpendicular sides 6 cm and 8 cm and hypotenuse 10 cm. Find its area.' Expected answers: ½; 8 cm and 3 cm, giving 12 cm²; 24 cm².

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse halving the base–height product and distinguishing perpendicular height from sloping side.

findings.finding: The cylinder topic does not review circle area and circumference before using them to develop surface area.
findings.breakdown: Students must distinguish the circumference that becomes the rectangle's length from the area of each circular end. A retrieval gap can become concealed inside the combined formula.
findings.checked: p18-net-flat-example supplies 2πr, and p18-circle-area-cloze requests symbolic circle area during formula development. Neither provides an opening numerical review of the two formulas. The preceding triangular-prism topic does not rehearse them.
findings.assumptions: Circle area and circumference are prior knowledge, consistent with the course's separate circle-area teaching. A calculator may be used; calculator evaluation is not the missing review piece.

repair.proposal: Before p18-net-definition, add: '1 Write the circumference formula for radius r. 2 Find the circumference when r = 3 cm. 3 Write the circle-area formula for radius r. 4 Find the area when r = 3 cm. 5 For radius 5 cm, find both circumference and area. Leave answers in terms of π and include units.' Expected answers: 2πr; 6π cm; πr²; 9π cm²; 10π cm and 25π cm².

findings.doneWhen: Students retrieve and distinguish both circle formulas before developing the cylinder formula.

findings.finding: Two worked examples substitute converted radius or diameter values without stating how the labelled dimension produces them.
findings.breakdown: p26 introduces 12 cm as the cut rectangle's width from a labelled radius of 6 cm. p30 introduces radius 3 cm from the labelled 6 cm width. These unwritten geometric decisions can encourage students to substitute the labelled value without identifying its role.
findings.checked: The substitutions are mathematically correct. p25-d asks for a symbolic top-rectangle expression, but its supplied answer is not a written derivation in the teaching. Earlier radius–diameter practice does not provide the missing connection within either worked example. The standard specifically requires that connection to be stated when the working substitutes a converted dimension.
findings.assumptions: Students know the radius–diameter relationship. Calculator use does not identify which dimension the surface calculation needs.

repair.proposal: Before 15 × 12 in p26-example-top-component, add: 'The top rectangle's width is the diameter: d = 2r = 2 × 6 = 12 cm.' Before the p30 component calculations, add: 'The semicircle has diameter 6 cm, so r = 6 ÷ 2 = 3 cm.'

findings.doneWhen: Each converted value is explicitly connected to the labelled dimension before substitution.

findings.finding: Generalise the surface area of a closed sector cylinder.
findings.breakdown: The task distinguishes the surfaces that scale with retained angle from the two radial rectangles whose dimensions remain fixed.
findings.checked: p26-guided-b establishes the two radial rectangles, and p29-q7 supplies the arc-length relationship and varied sector angles. For positive radius and length and 0 < θ < 360°, the proposed formula counts every exposed surface correctly.
findings.assumptions: r > 0, h > 0 and θ is the retained angle in degrees, with 0 < θ < 360.

repair.proposal: After p29-q7, optionally ask: 'A closed sector cylinder has radius r, length h and retained angle θ°, where r,h > 0 and 0 < θ < 360. Write its surface area and explain why multiplying the entire closed-cylinder formula by θ/360 is insufficient.' Expected answer: SA = (θ/360)(2πr² + 2πrh) + 2rh. The ends and curved surface scale with angle; the two radial rectangles each contribute rh.

findings.doneWhen: Students explain both the angle-dependent contribution and the fixed contribution of the cut rectangles.

findings.finding: Explain why removing a rectangular corner reduces end area while preserving cross-sectional perimeter.
findings.breakdown: The task connects the L-shaped example with the area and complete-boundary terms in SA = 2B + ph.
findings.checked: p33-q6 supplies the general surface-area formula and an L-shaped prism. Removing a corner replaces boundary lengths a and b with equal inner lengths, so perimeter is unchanged; the two end areas together decrease by 2ab.
findings.assumptions: W,H,L > 0; 0 < a < W and 0 < b < H. The corner is removed through the prism's full length.

repair.proposal: After p33-q6-d, optionally ask: 'Remove a rectangular corner of width a and height b through the full length L of a rectangular prism with cross-section W by H, where 0 < a < W and 0 < b < H. Predict whether the cross-sectional perimeter changes, then justify your answer. How does total surface area change?' Expected answer: perimeter remains 2(W + H), because the removed boundary lengths are replaced by equal inner lengths. End area decreases by ab, so total surface area decreases by 2ab.

findings.doneWhen: Students explain the unchanged perimeter and derive the decrease of 2ab in surface area.

findings.finding: The first tunnel tasks introduce exposed internal walls without explaining that these surfaces count.
findings.breakdown: Students may subtract the openings but omit the tunnel walls, extending the earlier exclusion of internal joins to surfaces exposed inside a tunnel.
findings.checked: p33-q6 supplies SA = 2B + ph, so another area-calculation method is unnecessary. However, its examples do not expose a closed inner boundary. p25 treats cut surfaces and p30 and p35 exclude joins; none distinguishes an exposed tunnel wall from an excluded contact surface. p38-q3 explicitly includes the inside, but appears after both targeted tasks.
findings.assumptions: The tunnels pass through the full stated length. Students already know rectangular area and the existing surface-area methods. Calculator availability does not affect surface selection.

repair.proposal: Before p38-part-e, add: 'Include the exposed walls inside each tunnel. Remove the opening area from both end faces and add the four tunnel-wall rectangles. A rectangular tunnel of width w, height h and length L has wall area 2wL + 2hL. These exposed walls count; joined contact surfaces do not.'

findings.doneWhen: Before attempting either tunnel task, students are explicitly prompted to count its exposed internal walls.

findings.finding: Determine when drilling a circular tunnel increases a cylinder's surface area.
findings.breakdown: Students generalise the balance between removed end areas and added internal curved area.
findings.checked: p38-q3 explicitly includes the hollow cylinder's ends and inside. Removing two circles and adding the inner curved surface gives ΔSA = 2πrL − 2πr² = 2πr(L − r), so the proposed three cases are correct.
findings.assumptions: R,L > 0 and 0 < r < R; the tunnel runs along the cylinder's axis through both ends.

repair.proposal: After p38-q3, optionally ask: 'A closed cylinder has radius R and length L. A circular tunnel of radius r, where 0 < r < R, is drilled along its axis through both ends. When does its surface area increase, remain unchanged or decrease? Explain using the areas removed and added.' Expected answer: ΔSA = 2πr(L − r); area increases when L > r, is unchanged when L = r and decreases when L < r.

findings.doneWhen: Students derive the change in surface area and explain all three conditions.

protectedGroups.observation: Moving the triangular ends along the rectangular strip can produce another net of the same triangular prism.
protectedGroups.varies: The rectangle to which the triangular ends attach.
protectedGroups.invariant: The three rectangular lateral faces, two congruent triangular ends and resulting solid.

protectedGroups.observation: Pythagoras requires addition for an unknown hypotenuse and subtraction for an unknown shorter side.
protectedGroups.varies: The role of the unknown side, with the transition explicitly signalled.
protectedGroups.invariant: A right-triangular cross-section followed by the same five-face surface-area calculation.

protectedGroups.observation: The half-base construction supports finding either a sloping side or the perpendicular altitude.
protectedGroups.varies: Which length is unknown and how much of the construction is supplied.
protectedGroups.invariant: An isosceles triangular end divided into two right triangles.

protectedGroups.observation: Exchanging radius and height preserves curved surface area but changes the circular-end contribution and hence total area.
protectedGroups.varies: Radius and height exchange the values 5 cm and 3 cm.
protectedGroups.invariant: The product rh, closed-cylinder status and measurement units.

protectedGroups.observation: A 10% increase in height produces a smaller percentage increase in total surface area because the circular ends remain unchanged.
protectedGroups.varies: Height changes from 20 cm to 22 cm.
protectedGroups.invariant: Radius 12 cm and the area of the two circular ends.

protectedGroups.observation: A radius of 6 cm and a diameter of 12 cm describe equal circular faces; the cylinder task adds the second end and curved surface.
protectedGroups.varies: Radius versus diameter representation and circle area versus cylinder surface area.

protectedGroups.observation: The same axial-section Pythagoras method recovers a diameter across orientations and both exact and irrational intermediate lengths.
protectedGroups.invariant: Given cylinder height and axial diagonal; unknown diameter is recovered before radius and surface area.

protectedGroups.observation: Opening ends removes circular area while leaving the curved surface unchanged.
protectedGroups.varies: Number of closed circular ends: two, one, zero.
protectedGroups.invariant: Radius r, height h and full curved surface.

protectedGroups.observation: Opening the cut face and then one end removes only those component areas.
protectedGroups.varies: First the rectangular cut face is removed, then one semicircular end.
protectedGroups.invariant: Radius r, height h and half the full curved surface.
